title: Energy supply
summary: Where energy comes from in GCAM: graded fossil resources, renewable supply curves, power plants with levelised costs, and the value-factor rule that makes wind and solar dearer as they grow.
outcomes: You can compute a levelised cost of electricity with a carbon price
You can explain graded resource supply curves
You can describe the value-factor method for wind and solar (v7.3 onward)
You can name where GCAM's technology cost assumptions live
narration_en: Energy supply in GCAM starts in the ground and in the sky. Coal, oil, gas and uranium are depletable resources described by graded supply curves: the cheap grades are used first, and the price climbs as more is extracted. Wind and solar are flows rather than stocks, described by renewable supply curves. These primary resources feed conversion sectors such as power plants, refineries and hydrogen production. Each technology has a cost built from three parts: a non-energy cost that covers building and running the plant, a fuel cost, and an emissions cost under any carbon price. In this module you will compute a levelised cost of electricity for a gas plant and a solar farm, and see the gas cost rise by about eighteen dollars for every fifty dollars of carbon price. You will also meet the value factor. As wind and solar take a larger share of the grid, each extra unit is worth less, so GCAM divides their cost by a value factor that falls with market share. That simple rule keeps renewables from taking over unrealistically fast.
narration_ar: يبدأ إمداد الطاقة في نموذج GCAM من باطن الأرض ومن السماء. الفحم والنفط والغاز واليورانيوم موارد ناضبة تصفها منحنيات عرض متدرجة: تُستخدم الدرجات الرخيصة أولًا، ويرتفع السعر كلما استُخرج المزيد. أما الرياح والشمس فهي تدفقات لا مخزونات، وتصفها منحنيات عرض للطاقة المتجددة. تغذي هذه الموارد الأولية قطاعات التحويل مثل محطات الكهرباء والمصافي وإنتاج الهيدروجين. ولكل تقنية تكلفة من ثلاثة أجزاء: تكلفة غير طاقية تغطي بناء المحطة وتشغيلها، وتكلفة الوقود، وتكلفة الانبعاثات في ظل أي سعر للكربون. في هذه الوحدة ستحسب التكلفة المستوية للكهرباء لمحطة غاز ولمزرعة شمسية، وترى تكلفة الغاز ترتفع بنحو ثمانية عشر دولارًا لكل خمسين دولارًا من سعر الكربون. وستتعرف أيضًا على معامل القيمة. فكلما أخذت الرياح والشمس حصة أكبر من الشبكة قلّت قيمة كل وحدة إضافية، لذلك يقسم النموذج تكلفتهما على معامل قيمة ينخفض مع الحصة السوقية. هذه القاعدة البسيطة تمنع الطاقة المتجددة من السيطرة بسرعة غير واقعية.

diagram.title: From resources to delivered electricity
diagram.caption: Resources feed conversion technologies; each technology's cost includes fuel and carbon, and wind/solar get a value-factor adjustment.

nodes.label: Fossil resources
nodes.detail: Coal, oil, gas, uranium: graded curves inside a resource/reserve model; cheap grades first, price rises with use (supply_energy.html). Files A11.fos_curves.csv, A12.U_curves.csv.

nodes.label: Renewable resources
nodes.detail: Annual flows with supply curves Q = max·P^b/(Mid^b + P^b). Hydropower is exogenous fixed output; utility solar is nearly unlimited at low price (supply_energy.html).

nodes.label: Bioenergy
nodes.detail: Purpose-grown energy crops, residues and waste come from the land module and compete with food for land.

nodes.label: Power plants
nodes.detail: Non-energy cost is levelised: overnight capital × capital recovery factor ÷ capacity factor + O&M. Costs from NREL ATB, updated in v8.8 (en_technologies.html).

nodes.label: Value factor
nodes.detail: Since v7.3 wind and solar cost is divided by a value factor that falls linearly with market share, e.g. PV intercept 0.972, slope −1.443 (CMP 394).

nodes.label: Carbon capture
nodes.detail: CCS is a remove-fraction on a technology's emissions, sent to a storage market (en_technologies.html).

nodes.label: Electricity market
nodes.detail: Technologies share the electricity market by nested logit; the solved price feeds buildings, industry and transport.

nodes.label: Carbon price
nodes.detail: Adds emission factor × carbon price to each technology's cost.

tour.text: Fossil fuels come from graded curves: the more you extract, the higher the cost of the next grade.
Renewables are flows with their own curves; bioenergy arrives from the land module.
Each plant's cost = non-energy (capital, O&M) + fuel ÷ efficiency + emissions cost.
A carbon price adds emission factor × price: gas rises ~$18/MWh per $50/t in the kit example.
Wind and solar cost is divided by a value factor that shrinks as their share grows, slowing their growth.
CCS sends captured CO₂ to storage; technologies share the electricity market by logit.

sections.heading: Resources: stocks and flows
sections.html:
Depletable resources (coal, oil, unconventional oil, gas, uranium) sit on graded supply curves: as the price rises, more of the resource becomes economic. Technical change can lower extraction costs over time (supply_energy.html). In the kit's toy curve, cost rises from $3/GJ to $12/GJ across four grades, so the price at 200, 800 and 1400 EJ of cumulative use is 3.6, 6.0 and 11.0 $/GJ.

Renewables are annual flows:

Q = Qmax · Pb / (Pmidb + Pb)

where Pmid is the price at which half the maximum is produced.

sections.heading: Technology cost
sections.html:
Every technology's cost per unit of output is

C = non-energy cost + Σ (input price × input coefficient) + Σ (GHG price × emissions) − secondary output value

For power plants, non-energy cost is levelised: overnight capital × capital recovery factor ÷ (capacity factor × 8.76) + fixed and variable O&M (en_technologies.html). The kit's gas plant (capex $1,000/kW, capacity factor 0.55, fuel $6/GJ, efficiency 55%) costs 61.2 $/MWh with no carbon price, 79.5 at $50/t and 97.9 at $100/t. The solar farm (capex $900/kW, CF 0.22) costs 45.4 $/MWh at any carbon price. Illustrative numbers.

sections.heading: Wind and solar: the value factor
sections.html:
Since v7.3 GCAM no longer pairs wind and solar with backup turbines. Instead their levelised cost is divided by a value factor that falls linearly with their market share (CMP 394):

PLCOE = LCOE / VF, VF = intercept + slope × share

For PV the intercept is 0.972 and the slope −1.443 (then divided by 0.903, the non-VRE average); onshore wind 0.91 and −1.2. The relationships come from ReEDS for the contiguous US and may break down above about 75% VRE. Storage is not modelled explicitly.

sections.heading: Electricity, fuels and hydrogen
sections.html: Electricity is nested: fuel subsector → technology → cooling system (up to five types). Refining covers oil, biomass liquids (up to 8 technologies per region, some with CCS), coal-to-liquids and gas-to-liquids. Hydrogen has 10 central and 2 forecourt routes from up to 7 primary sources. CCS is a remove-fraction on emissions sent to a storage market; direct air capture enters with a share weight rising to 1 by 2050 (supply_energy.html, details_energy.html).

sections.heading: Vintages and retirement
sections.html: Plants built in one period keep running: GCAM tracks vintages. Three shutdown rules exist: profit shutdown (output falls as variable cost approaches price), an S-curve lifetime, and exogenous output scalars, such as a 2015 US coal plant at 0.5 in 2021 falling to 0 by 2040 (en_technologies.html). This is why the fleet changes more slowly than new investment.

callouts.title: In GCAM
callouts.html: Power plant costs come from NREL ATB files (NREL_ATB_capital.csv, NREL_ATB_OMfixed.csv, NREL_ATB_OMvar.csv); efficiencies, capture rates and retirement in A23.globaltech_*.csv (inputs_supply.html). Units: capital-overnight in 1975$/kW, prices in 1975$/GJ. Query elec gen by subsector to see the mix. Plant-specific values are not printed on the doc pages.

callouts.title: A useful mental model
callouts.html: The first solar farm in a region sells power at midday when it is valuable. The hundredth floods the same hours and earns less. The value factor charges that crowding as a higher effective cost.

callouts.title: "GCAM learns: costs fall as capacity grows"
callouts.html: In the released model, future technology costs are inputs you choose; the model does not learn during a run. Learning curves are one way to write those inputs (the kit computes $900/kW falling to $460.8/kW after three doublings at 20%).

takeaways: Fossil fuels come from graded supply curves; renewables from flow supply curves
Technology cost = non-energy cost + fuel cost + emissions cost
A carbon price raises each option's cost in proportion to its emissions
Wind and solar costs are divided by a value factor that falls with their share (v7.3+)
Future costs are inputs, not learned by the model; vintages make the fleet change slowly

quiz.q: In GCAM v8.2/9.1, the integration cost of wind and solar is represented by…
options: a backup turbine for every VRE plant
a value factor that falls with market share
quiz.explain: PLCOE = LCOE / VF since v7.3; storage is not explicit.

quiz.q: The kit gas plant costs 61.2 $/MWh at zero carbon price and 79.5 at $50/t. At $100/t it costs about…
A graded resource supply curve means…
options: all of the resource costs the same
cheap grades are used first, so price rises with use
the price falls as you use more
quiz.explain: Higher grades are dearer to extract.

quiz.q: Does GCAM compute technology learning during a run?
options: No: future costs are input assumptions
quiz.explain: Costs are inputs; learning curves can be used to choose them.
